checks.prompt: A team maintains four internal agent applications and has wrapped six data sources (their issue tracker, warehouse, wiki, deploy log, on-call rota and CI) for each of them separately. A seventh source arrives. Under their current arrangement, how much new integration work does that seventh source create, how much would it create if the six had been exposed the way this technique exposes them, and which single property of the arrangement causes the difference?
checks.explanation: The whole argument for the protocol is an arithmetic one. With M consumers and N capabilities and no shared contract you write M×N adapters, and each new capability costs M of them. Putting the capability behind a protocol every consumer speaks makes it M+N: the seventh source is one piece of work, and it lights up in every host that speaks the protocol. Nothing about the encoding alone would achieve that — the saving comes from the consumers sharing one contract, not from JSON-RPC being tidy.
options: Four wrappers now, one afterwards. The cause is that the capability is moved behind a protocol every application already speaks, so a source is written once against the protocol instead of once per consumer — the number of pieces of glue stops being applications times sources and becomes applications plus sources

Four wrappers now and four afterwards. The protocol standardises the message encoding but each application still needs its own adapter, so the saving is in the wire format rather than in the number of integrations
Six wrappers now, one afterwards. The count is driven by the sources already integrated, because a new source must be reconciled against each existing one before the applications can see it
One wrapper now, one afterwards. The applications already share a tool abstraction, so the integration count never depended on how many applications there were

checks.prompt: A developer building a documentation server puts the model call inside the server: their `search_docs` server loads the corpus, calls an LLM with its own API key to rerank the hits, and returns a written summary. Their host application is now slow, the server needs a paid key deployed alongside it, and users complain that the assistant 'won't take direction' about how results are presented. Name the architectural inversion they have violated, explain what each of the three roles in this architecture is responsible for, and describe the protocol feature that lets a server obtain a completion without owning any of this.
checks.expected: A correct answer must name the inversion: the server provides capabilities and the host (which owns the model) decides whether, when and how to use them. Intelligence lives in the host; the server is deliberately 'dumb and honest' — it answers protocol requests and does not reason. Putting model logic in the server inverts that, which is why the host lost control of presentation: the reranking and summarising decisions were made behind a boundary the host cannot see or influence, so the host can no longer steer them. The three roles must be distinguished: the HOST is the application the user interacts with, embeds the LLM and decides what to expose to it; the CLIENT is a connector living inside the host, one per connected server, maintaining a 1:1 session with it; the SERVER is a separate program exposing capabilities, which does not call the model. The answer must name sampling as the feature: when a server genuinely needs a completion it asks the host for one through the protocol, so the credential, the model choice and the cost stay with the host — which also removes the second key from the deployment. Noting that the separate process is what gives the server its own permissions and credentials, or that the analogy is the editor/language-server split where one server works in every editor, is a plus.

checks.prompt: Three capabilities are being designed for one server: (a) fetching the current rows of a database table so the assistant can reason over them, with no side effects; (b) opening a pull request; (c) a parameterised 'summarise this release' workflow the user picks from a menu. Classify each into one of the protocol's three server-side primitives, and state which party decides that each is used.
checks.explanation: The three primitives are separated by who is in control, not by what they happen to return. Tools are model-controlled functions and are where side effects belong. Resources are application-controlled read-only data addressed by URI — the host decides what to load into context, like a GET. Prompts are user-controlled templates the user invokes deliberately. Collapsing them into one call throws that control distinction away, which is the thing the split exists to express.
options: (a) is a resource, chosen by the application: read-only data addressed by a URI that the host loads into context. (b) is a tool, chosen by the model: a function with side effects that the model decides to invoke. (c) is a prompt, chosen by the user: a reusable parameterised template the user explicitly invokes
All three are tools, and the difference is only whether the tool is marked read-only; the model decides all three because everything a server exposes is reachable through the same call
(a) is a resource and (b) is a tool, both chosen by the model, while (c) is a resource whose URI names the template — the user never selects a primitive directly
(a) is a prompt chosen by the application, (b) is a tool chosen by the user because side effects need consent, and (c) is a resource chosen by the model when it decides a summary is wanted

checks.prompt: Implement `serve(requests, tools)`, a self-contained server for the subset of the protocol a session actually uses. `requests` is a list of JSON-RPC 2.0 message dicts to process in order against ONE session; `tools` maps a tool name to `{"description": str, "inputSchema": dict, "fn": callable}`. Return the list of response dicts, each `{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": <the request's id>, ...}` plus either a `"result"` or an `"error"` of `{"code": int, "message": str}`. Rules: a message with no `"id"` key is a notification and produces NO response at all, whatever else the rules below say about it. Until an `initialize` has succeeded, every other method is refused with code -32600 and the message "server not initialized"; a second `initialize` on a live session is refused with -32600 too. `initialize` results carry `protocolVersion`, `capabilities` (advertise `{"tools": {}}`) and `serverInfo` with a `name` and `version`; define `SUPPORTED = ("2025-06-18", "2025-03-26")` at module level, echo the client's requested `params["protocolVersion"]` when the server speaks it and otherwise answer with `SUPPORTED[0]`. `tools/list` returns `{"tools": [...]}` where each entry carries exactly `name`, `description` and `inputSchema`. `tools/call` takes `params["name"]` and `params["arguments"]`, and returns `{"content": [{"type": "text", "text": str(value)}], "isError": False}`; if the tool function RAISES, that is not a protocol error — return the same result shape with `isError` True and the exception's text, so the model can read the failure. An unknown tool name is an error with code -32602, and any other method is -32601 with the message "Method not found: <method>". Standard library only.
checks.explanation: Four separate ideas are being asserted, and each is a place implementations really go wrong. The handshake is a gate, not a formality: the identical call is refused before it and served after, which is why you cannot skip straight to invoking a tool. A notification is defined by the absence of an id, and the correct handling is silence — an error reply to a notification is itself a protocol violation. Version negotiation means answering with a version you actually speak rather than parroting whatever arrived. And the sharpest one: a tool that raises is reported in band, as a successful response whose payload says it failed, because the model needs to see that text and decide what to do; a method the server does not implement is a protocol error, which the transport layer handles and the model never sees. Note also that publishing the tool list means publishing the schema, not the callable — the entries carry exactly the three declared keys.
checks.test:
def tools():
    return {
        "add": {
            "description": "Add two numbers.",
            "inputSchema": {"type": "object",
                            "properties": {"a": {"type": "number"},
                                           "b": {"type": "number"}},
                            "required": ["a", "b"]},
            "fn": lambda a, b: a + b,
        },
        "explode": {
            "description": "Always fails.",
            "inputSchema": {"type": "object", "properties": {}},
            "fn": lambda: (_ for _ in ()).throw(RuntimeError("disk on fire")),
        },
    }


INIT = {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize",
        "params": {"protocolVersion": "2025-06-18", "capabilities": {}}}

# The lifecycle is the point: a call that arrives before the handshake is refused,
# and the very same call succeeds once initialize has completed.
early = serve([{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 9, "method": "tools/call",
                "params": {"name": "add", "arguments": {"a": 1, "b": 2}}}], tools())
assert len(early) == 1, early
assert "error" in early[0] and "result" not in early[0], early[0]
assert early[0]["error"]["code"] == -32600, early[0]
assert early[0]["id"] == 9 and early[0]["jsonrpc"] == "2.0", early[0]

ok = serve([INIT, {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 9, "method": "tools/call",
                   "params": {"name": "add", "arguments": {"a": 1, "b": 2}}}], tools())
assert len(ok) == 2, ok
assert ok[1]["result"]["content"] == [{"type": "text", "text": "3"}], ok[1]
assert ok[1]["result"]["isError"] is False, ok[1]

# A notification carries no id and therefore no reply -- not even an error one.
quiet = serve([{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "notifications/initialized"}], tools())
assert quiet == [], quiet
assert len(serve([INIT, {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "method": "tools/list"}], tools())) == 1

# initialize answers with the negotiated version and the advertised capabilities.
first = serve([INIT], tools())[0]["result"]
assert first["protocolVersion"] == "2025-06-18", first
assert "tools" in first["capabilities"], first
assert set(first["serverInfo"]) >= {"name", "version"}, first

# A version the server does not speak is answered with one it does, not echoed back.
old = serve([{"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "initialize",
              "params": {"protocolVersion": "1999-01-01"}}], tools())[0]["result"]
assert old["protocolVersion"] in SUPPORTED and old["protocolVersion"] != "1999-01-01", old

# A second handshake on a live session is an error, not a reset.
again = serve([INIT, INIT], tools())
assert "error" in again[1], again

# tools/list publishes the schema and nothing the host cannot serialise.
listed = serve([INIT, {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 2, "method": "tools/list"}], tools())
entries = listed[1]["result"]["tools"]
assert {e["name"] for e in entries} == {"add", "explode"}, entries
for entry in entries:
    assert set(entry) == {"name", "description", "inputSchema"}, entry
    assert entry["inputSchema"]["type"] == "object", entry

# A tool that raises is reported IN BAND, so the model can read and retry it;
# an unknown method is a protocol error, which the model never sees.
boom = serve([INIT, {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 3, "method": "tools/call",
                     "params": {"name": "explode", "arguments": {}}}], tools())[1]
assert "result" in boom and "error" not in boom, boom
assert boom["result"]["isError"] is True, boom
assert "disk on fire" in boom["result"]["content"][0]["text"], boom

missing = serve([INIT, {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 4, "method": "resources/read"}], tools())[1]
assert "error" in missing and missing["error"]["code"] == -32601, missing

unknown = serve([INIT, {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 5, "method": "tools/call",
                        "params": {"name": "nope", "arguments": {}}}], tools())[1]
assert "error" in unknown, unknown

# Ids come back on the responses that have them, in order.
many = serve([INIT, {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": "tools/list"},
              {"jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 8, "method": "tools/call",
               "params": {"name": "add", "arguments": {"a": 20, "b": 22}}}], tools())
assert [r["id"] for r in many] == [1, 7, 8], many
assert many[2]["result"]["content"][0]["text"] == "42", many[2]

checks.prompt: A local server, launched as a child process by the host, works perfectly under unit tests but the host reports parse errors as soon as it connects. The author has added `print()` calls for tracing and imported a library that logs to standard output on startup. Separately, the author is puzzled that the model keeps calling `fetch_data` when it should call `search_issues`, even though both are registered correctly. What are the two causes?
checks.explanation: Two independent traps. When the server is a child process, its standard output IS the wire — the frames and your debugging share one stream, so the debugging has to move to standard error, including any dependency's logging. And tool selection is a language problem, not a wiring problem: the model sees only the name, the description and the schema, so those strings are prompts you are writing for a model, and vagueness in them shows up as the wrong tool being called or none at all.
options: The transport for a local child process frames its messages over standard output, so any other write into that stream corrupts it — tracing must go to standard error instead, and a dependency that logs to stdout has to be reconfigured. The tool selection problem is that the model chooses purely from the name, description and schema it is shown: those strings are prompt engineering, and a vague description gets the wrong tool called

The parse errors come from not flushing standard output after each frame, so tracing is fine as long as it is flushed; the tool selection problem is that the two tools were registered in the wrong order, and the model prefers the first tool it is shown

The parse errors mean the protocol version was not negotiated, and the tracing is a red herring; the tool selection problem is that tool descriptions are ignored by the model, which dispatches on the schema alone, so the fix is to make the argument names more distinct
Both problems have the same cause: the server is stateful across reconnects, so a stale session is being reused — restarting the host clears the corrupted stream and the mis-registered tools together

checks.prompt: Argue the boundary for three cases. (a) A single internal chat app has one helper function that parses its own log format, tightly coupled to its internals. (b) A company wants its incident-history store readable by its IDE assistant, its chat assistant and a nightly triage agent, each running with different credentials. (c) Two independently owned autonomous agents — one that plans travel, one that books it — need to hand work to each other. For each, say whether this technique is the right layer and what to use instead if not, and then explain why the answer to (a) is not simply 'always use the protocol, it is more general'.
checks.expected: A correct answer must place all three and give the reason for each. (a) Not this technique: one function inside one application, coupled to that application's internals, is served by the model provider's own function-calling / tool-use loop. There is no reuse to win and no trust boundary to draw, so the protocol only adds a process boundary and a protocol layer. (b) This technique: the deciding properties are that more than one consumer wants the same capability and that each should run with its own permissions, which is exactly what a separately-hosted server with its own credentials gives — write it once, and all three hosts speak to it. (c) Not this technique: agent-to-agent communication is a different layer. This protocol connects an agent to tools and data; a peer protocol for autonomous agents handles agent-to-agent delegation, and the two compose rather than compete. The justification for (a) must engage with cost rather than dismiss the question: generality is not free, and the concrete price is a separate process to launch and supervise, a protocol round trip on every call, and a schema to maintain for a function whose only caller is in the same process — so the rule of thumb is that a capability which should be usable by more than one client, or which needs its own permissions, becomes a server, and a single function inside a single application does not. Noting that the two are complementary — a server is how a tool is DELIVERED, while the provider's function-calling loop is how it is INVOKED — is a plus, as is noting that framework-native tool abstractions increasingly consume these servers rather than replacing them.
